questions.stem: A 45-year-old healthcare worker received a needlestick injury. The recipient was known to be a hepatitis B vaccine non-responder despite two vaccination courses. Recipient: HBsAg negative Hepatitis B surface antibody 2 mIU/mL HBV cAb negative Source: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBeAb negative HBV DNA 62 million U/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: A single dose of hepatitis B vaccine
An accelerated course of hepatitis B vaccination
Single dose of HBIG and an accelerated course of hepatitis B vaccine
Two doses of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) 1 month apart

questions.explanation: Two doses of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) 1 month apart The healthcare worker has no immunity to hepatitis B and has sustained a significant exposure to a patient who is HBsAg+ and thus requires immediate intervention. The CDC recommend that nonresponders should preferably receive two doses of HBIG 1 month apart as postexposure prophylaxis. Adequate protection against infection would not be provided by the alternative options. If the recipient’s anti-HBsAb status is unknown, then the CDC recommend a single dose of HBIG and commencing a course of HBV vaccination.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q44

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman was reviewed with a new diagnosis of HIV and hepatitis B co-infection. A pregnancy test was negative. Despite multiple educational meetings she declined HIV treatment but was interested in hepatitis B treatment. Investigations: AST 89 IU/L ALT 98 units/L CD4 count 434 cells/μL HIV viral load 55,000 copies/mL HBsAg positive HBV viral load 540,000 IU/mL Liver biopsy showed significant fibrosis but no cirrhosis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to offer?
questions.explanation: Peginterferon alfa 2B The patient is refusing HIV treatment at this time. The concern is that using an agent for her hepatitis that also has activity against HIV would lead to the development of HIV resistance. Entecavir, lamivudine, tenofovir, and emtricitabine are all active against both HIV and HBV . Only peginterferon alfa 2B alone will not lead to HIV-resistance. Remember that interferon therapy has many disadvantages, multiple side effects (i.e., influenza-like syndrome, myalgias, depression, fatigue, etc.) and is only given IM. If the patient would have accepted treatment for both HIV and HBV , then combination therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir would have been the optimal choice. This regimen offers three active drugs against HIV as recommended by the DHHS guidelines and at the same time would offer two active drugs against hepatitis B (tenofovir and emtricitabine).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q8

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and 10 days of jaundice. She was an active IV drug user. On physical exam, she was jaundiced with right upper quadrant tenderness. Investigations: ALT 2000 IU/mL AST 900 IU/mL HAV IgM negative, HAV PCR negative HCV IgG negative, HCV PCR negative HBVsAg positive, anti-HBs negative anti-HBc IgM positive, anti-HBc total positive HBe Ag positive, anti-HBe negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute hepatitis B Hepatitis C and Hepatitis A testing are both negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is a marker for active replication signifying that the patient is infectious. It is present in high amounts during the acute phase of infection. It can also be present during the chronic phase of infection if the immune system fails to clear the virus effectively. If HBsAg is present at all the patient should be considered contagious. If it is present for 6 months or more the patient is considered to have chronic hepatitis B. Differentiation between chronic replicating and chronic, nonreplicating is the presence of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBe antibodies. In chronic, replicating hepatitis B the patient will be positive for HBeAg; during chronic, nonreplicating infection anti-HBe antibodies will be present. In both chronic conditions the total core antibody (anti-HBc) will be positive while anti-HBc IgM will be negative. If NAAT testing is performed during this time the amount of HBV DNA will be higher during chronic, replicating hepatitis B. This person is in the acute phase of infection as the HBsAg is positive and no antibodies to the surface antigen have been generated. In addition, the total and IgM core (HBc) antibodies are present, as is the case in acute hepatitis B.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q3

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with jaundice, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. She was 22/40 weeks pregnant. She was sexually active and was not using condoms. She had received a blood transfusion for anemia 2 weeks prior to this admission. She was a nurse at a local physician’s office and had received all recommended vaccinations 5 years ago when she started working. Investigations: ALT 750 IU/L AST 2320 IU/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus Both hepatitis B and herpes simplex virus infection can cause a fulminant hepatitis. She is unlikely to get HBV as she is vaccinated. Herpes simplex has been described to more commonly cause fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy. Hepatitis G virus (GBV-C) is transmitted by transfusion but does not cause any known disease. CMV can cause a mild hepatitis, but HSV would more commonly cause fulminant hepatitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q12

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presented with nausea, anorexia, and right upper quadrant pain. He was known to have coinfection with HIV and hepatitis B. He recently switched his HIV antiretroviral therapy from tenofovir/emtricitabine/ efavirenz to abacavir/lamivudine and raltegravir due to concerns over worsening renal function. He was sexually active and reported 4 casual male partners in the last 6 months, without using condoms. He had not traveled outside of the United States and had never used recreational intravenous drugs. On physical exam, he had scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly of 3 cm. Investigations: CD4 count 520 cells/μL HIV viral load <20 copies/mL AST 1623 U/L ALT 824 U/L Total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL (0.1–1.2) Hepatitis C IgG negative Hepatitis B surface antigen positive Hepatitis B core IgM positive HLAB5701 negative Right upper quadrant sonogram demonstrated no gallstones or biliary duct dilation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus flare In this patient with HIV–HBV co-infection, the most likely cause of the acute hepatitis is a flare of the chronic hepatitis B precipitated by the change from a tenofovir-based ART to one containing lamivudine. Monotherapy with lamivudine for HBV is not recommended due to the risk of drug resistance and an acute flare in HBV . This is also supported by the positive HBV core IgM which often is seen in flares. Drug-induced liver injury from the current ART is less likely and fails to explain the hepatitis B virus serologies. Hepatitis D virus is most closely associated with IVDA or travel to areas of endemicity such as the Mediterranean basin. HIV cholangiopathy and MAC are primarily seen in patients with advanced AIDS and CD4 <50–100.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q23

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with confusion. He had been discharged 3 days earlier after recovering from an episode of acute hepatitis and jaundice. He was an active intravenous drug user. Investigations: Day 1 Day 7 Day 10 AST (IU/L) 1200 – 2200 ALT (IU/L) 1500 180 3000 INR 1.2 – 3.5 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 0.9 – 5.4 Serology HAV IgM negative HBV sAg positive HBV cAb IgM positive HCV Ab negative HBV sAg positive HBV DNA positive HCV RNA negative HIV Ag/Ab negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Acute HCV superimposed on chronic HBV

questions.explanation: Co-infection with HBV and HDV The timing is most consistent with co-infection with HBV and HDV , which is more likely to present with worsening liver disease. The serologies are not consistent with acute infection with either HAV or HCV but are consistent with acute HBV infection, which initially improved. Acute HIV infection does not cause a fulminant hepatitis, although it can raise transaminases.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q25

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was being treated for hepatitis C with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. Investigations: HAV IgG positive HBV cAb positive, HBV sAg negative, HBV sAb 0 HBV DNA undetectable A B HCV IgG positive, HCV genotype 1a Liver biopsy showed grade 1 inflammation and stage 3 fibrosis with features of both chronic HCV and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Baseline Week 4 Week 11 ALT (IU/L) 170 35 2250 AST (IU/L) 289 32 2970 HCV viral load (IU/mL) 1,200,000 Undetectable Undetectable INR 1.8 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 7.2
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely reason for the worsening transaminases?
questions.explanation: Reactivation of HBV Reactivation of HBV in a patient with co-infection with HBV and HCV has been reported in patients being treated for HCV . A patient responding to HCV treatment who has a flare of hepatitis, but still with undetectable HCV viral loads, should be evaluated for HBV . Drug reaction is possible but rarely causes transaminases this elevated. For more information, see https://www.hhs.gov/hepatitis/blog/2017/1/17/hbv-reactivation-during-hcv-treatmen t.html
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q25

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Window period of acute hepatitis B – anti-HBc (IgM) is the sole marker between disappearance of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs. (2) Remote/resolved past infection with decline of anti-HBs (and/or HBsAg) below the limit of detection. (3) Occult chronic HBV infection – HBsAg fallen below detection with low-level HBV DNA replication.
b) (1) HBV DNA by PCR (distinguishes window-period/occult infection from resolved infection). (2) IgM anti-HBc to exclude/confirm acute infection; repeat full serology first to exclude false positive.

questions.question: A treatment-naive HIV-infected patient has virus carrying the K103N mutation. He takes a proton pump inhibitor, has chronic hepatitis B, and has had a prior myocardial infarction.
questions.question_raw: 2. HIV infected patient with HIV that has K103N mutation in treatment naive patient on PPI and with chronic hepB and prior MI.

parts.text: What is the appropriate initial regimen?
Name two initial drugs not appropriate for this patient and justify.
What three non-infectious issues must be monitored in him?

parts_raw.text: A. What is appropriate initial regimen?
B.  Name two initial drugs not appropriate for this patient and justify.
C. What three non infectious issues must be monitored in him?

questions.model_answer:
a) Dolutegravir plus tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine once daily (bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine or raltegravir + tenofovir-emtricitabine are equivalent alternatives): an INSTI avoids the NNRTI class inactivated by K103N, tenofovir + emtricitabine also treats his chronic HBV, and no abacavir is used given his coronary disease. INSTIs need no boosting and have no PPI interaction.
b) (1) Efavirenz - K103N is the classic mutation conferring efavirenz (and nevirapine) resistance. (2) Abacavir - cohort data link abacavir to increased myocardial infarction rates, and caution is advised in patients with preexisting cardiac risk factors. (Rilpivirine and boosted atazanavir would equally be wrong choices because both require gastric acid/normal pH and are compromised by his PPI.)
c) (1) Renal function - serum creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis for glucose and protein, and serum phosphate on a tenofovir-containing regimen. (2) Bone mineral density - TDF causes bone loss; vitamin D and calcium supplementation mitigates it. (3) Cardiometabolic parameters - fasting lipid profile and fasting glucose/HbA1c given his prior MI (also monitor ALT/AST/bilirubin for hepatitis B-related flare and drug hepatotoxicity).

cohort_answer.text:
K103N mutation = NVP and EFV resistance; PPIs: avoid RVP and ATV/r; MI: avoid abacavir; Chronic Hep B = include 3TC / TDF. DTG/TDF/FTC; RAL/TDF/FTC; RAL/TAF/FTC

parts_raw.text: A.  What treatment?
B.  What test?
C.  When to start?

questions.model_answer:
a) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF, pregnancy category B) – the best-studied and preferred antiviral in pregnancy; lamivudine or telbivudine are alternatives.
b) HBV DNA (viral load) to determine the level of circulating viremia (and ALT/HBeAg to stage disease).
c) In the third trimester (~28–32 weeks) when HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL, to prevent perinatal transmission; women in the immunoactive phase are treated as non-pregnant women.
d) Infant receives hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) plus the first dose of HBV vaccine, both given within 12 hours of birth, and completes the vaccine series.

cohort_answer.text:
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate
If HepBs ag pos, check e ag, if pos then viral load, ALT
If e ag neg and viral load >200,000 IU/ml: start tx 24-32 weeks GA and continue till delivery or 12 weeks post partum; If e ag pos and viral load >20,000, start tx as per non pregnant person

questions.question: A GP recently vaccinated a patient for HBV and accidentally sends HBV serologies 2 days after: HBsAg positive, HBsAb negative, HBcAb total and IgM negative. Interpret.

parts.text: Interpret the serology.

parts_raw.text: Interpret.

questions.model_answer: Transient HBsAg positivity due to the recently administered HBV vaccine, not true infection. Recombinant vaccine contains HBsAg, which can be transiently detectable in serum for up to ~2–3 weeks after immunization; the absence of anti-HBc (total and IgM) and the vaccine timing exclude acute or chronic infection. Repeat testing after several weeks will show HBsAg clears and anti-HBs develops.

What two things are given to prevent HBV transmission?

parts_raw.text: How to prevent HIV transmission, list two mechanisms?
What two things are given to prevent HBV transmission?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Maternal suppressive antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy and intravenous intrapartum zidovudine when the viral load is unknown or >1000 copies/mL (with scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks if viral load >1000 copies/mL). (2) Infant antiretroviral prophylaxis started within 6 hours of birth — presumptive multidrug therapy (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir) in this high-risk, untreated-mother scenario — together with complete avoidance of breastfeeding where safe replacement feeding is available.
b) (1) Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and (2) hepatitis B vaccine, both given within 12 hours of birth, with the vaccine series completed and post-vaccination serology at 9-12 months.

questions.question: A pregnant woman without prenatal care has delivered her baby. She is found to have HIV and hepatitis B.

parts.text: What are two methods to prevent HIV transmission to baby?
2 methods to prevent HBV transmission to baby.

parts_raw.text: What are two methods to prevent HIV transmission to baby?
2 methods to prevent HBV transmission to baby.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Maternal antiretroviral therapy, including intravenous zidovudine intrapartum (2 mg/kg IV loading dose, then 1 mg/kg/h until the cord is clamped) and ongoing combination ART; because she is HBV coinfected, her regimen should contain a tenofovir prodrug (TDF or TAF) plus lamivudine or emtricitabine. (2) Infant antiretroviral prophylaxis started as soon as possible after delivery, together with avoidance of breastfeeding where formula feeding is safe.
b) (1) Passive immunization with hepatitis B immune globulin given to the newborn as soon as possible after birth. (2) Active immunization with the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine at birth, completing the series; her own maternal tenofovir-lamivudine/emtricitabine-containing ART also suppresses HBV replication.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC/PHAC perinatal HBV guidance: HBIG plus the birth dose of HBV vaccine at separate sites within 12 hours of birth, with post-vaccination serology at 9-12 months; the chapter does not cover neonatal HBIG.

cohort_answer.text: HIV prevention: Antepartum ART ASAP (tenofovir + lamivudine/FTC if HIV/HBV co-infected); intrapartum C-section at 38 weeks if unsuppressed; neonatal AZT or combination ARV if high risk; postpartum no breastfeeding, ARV (AZT, nevirapine, lamivudine) x6 weeks. For the dyslipidemia, choose TAF-based or, if lipids dominate, TDF-based dosing (TDF is associated with lower lipids, TAF with less renal/bone toxicity) and avoid a boosted PI, which commonly causes dyslipidemia and insulin resistance — use an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir or bictegravir) as the third agent; avoid abacavir given cardiovascular concerns and its lack of anti-HBV activity. cohort_answer.text: A) TDF is preferred: "Because it has extensive safety data and a lack of resistance in HBV, TDF is the preferred NA for pregnant women and those with child-bearing potential." B) HBsAg in the first trimester. Those documented to be HBsAg positive require subsequent testing for HBeAg, anti-Hbe, HBV DNA quantification, ALT to assess their stage of disease. C) Typically start at 24-32 weeks to prevent MTCT transmission; start earlier if risk factors for preterm labor, multiple gestations, planned invasive procedures (amnio); start in 2nd trimester if high viral load (>10^9). Pregnant women with HBV DNA of more than 200,000 IU/mL should initiate antiviral therapy at 24-32 weeks (~28 weeks) of gestation to reduce the risk of vertical transmission; may stop at delivery or up to 12 weeks postpartum if given strictly to prevent MTCT. D) Baby should receive HBIg and HBV vaccine within 12h of birth (with second and third doses of vaccine at 1 and 6 months). E) Yes - follow up vaccine dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively. Babies should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs between 1 and 4 months after the last dose of vaccine to confirm that they are uninfected and immune. Check Baby's sAg and sAb; if positive, baby is infected with HBV. If negative but not immune, vaccinate again with 2 additional doses until sAb >10 (immune). F) Yes as long as mom's nipples aren't cracking. Hep B is found in breastmilk but even pre-vaccine era was not associated with transmission. C section not recommended, no effect on MTCT.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Resolved past HBV infection (HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs may have declined to undetectable). (2) Occult chronic HBV with HBsAg below the detection limit (or window-period/false-negative HBsAg). b) HBV carries high morbidity in renal transplantation because immunosuppression drives persistent viral replication and impairs HBsAg seroconversion. The risk of de-novo HBV transmission from an anti-HBc-positive donor is low overall (about 1-4%) and depends on recipient immunity: it is negligible if the recipient is anti-HBs positive, and no prophylaxis is needed for an immune recipient. For a non-immune recipient, check donor HBV DNA; if negative no prophylaxis is required, and if positive give nucleos(t)ide antiviral (or HBIG) prophylaxis. All such recipients should have HBV DNA, HBsAg and liver enzymes monitored every 3-6 months, receive nucleos(t)ide therapy if reactivation occurs before clinical hepatitis, and be counselled about transmission precautions.

Risks depend on whether or not recipient is sAb positive, and whether this persists post transplant. Overall risk of 0-5.2% quoted, with risk negligible if recipient immune. No prophylaxis needed if HBV immune recipient receives from anti-HBc positive donor. If non immune, can check donor DNA level. If negative, no prophylaxis needed. If positive, can give antiviral or HBIG prophylaxis for 6-12 mo. Should check liver enzymes, sAg and HBV DNA Q3mo for 12 mo, and then Q6mo indefinitely if sAg positive donor. From an infection control perspective, treat these recipients as if they have HBV e.g. counsel on sharing household items that can be contaminated with blood.
British transplant society: The HBcAb positive (HBsAg negative) donor liver can be used for any potential liver recipient. (1C) When the liver comes from a HBcAb positive donor and is given to a HBV immune or non-immune recipient, prophylactic lamivudine should be given from the time of transplantation, and should be continued indefinitely. questions.model_answer: a) (1) Waning anti-HBs titre in a previous responder (anti-HBs can fall below detection over time although immune memory usually persists). (2) Primary vaccine non-response (roughly <10% after a standard 3-dose series). b) Repeat anti-HBs, and test HBsAg and anti-HBc to exclude past or occult infection; obtain liver enzymes if infection is suspected. If all remain negative (anti-HBs <10 IU/L), give a booster dose or a second complete 3-dose series and re-test for seroconversion 1-2 months after completion.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific non-responder revaccination strategy (booster vs second series, high-dose/combined HAV-HBV vaccine) follows CDC/ACIP occupational HBV guidance rather than the Mandell text.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Waning immunity. Vaccine non-responder (< 10% with standard 3 dose series)

B: Repeat HBsAb, HBsAg, HBcAb and obtain liver enzymes. If all negative (i.e. anti-HBs < 10), would complete second series of 3 vaccines and test for seroconversion 1-2 months after completion of series. There is some evidence that non-responders exhibit a better response when HBV/HAV vaccine given e.g. Twinrix. JID 2008 PMID 18544037. If KNOWN to have responded previously, but then lost sAb and at risk (e.g. IHD), can consider single booster dose of vaccine - may also benefit from higher dose. Non-responders include advanced age, smoking/higher BMI, chronic disease like CKD and other immunosuppression, celiac disease, genetic HLA variants

questions.model_answer:
a) HBV DNA (viral load) by PCR.
b) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF, category B) first line; lamivudine or telbivudine are alternatives.
c) Third trimester (~28–32 weeks) when HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL, to prevent mother-to-child transmission.
d) (1) Tenofovir DF/AF – serum creatinine/renal function and bone mineral density. (2) Adefovir – serum creatinine/renal function. (3) Entecavir – HBV DNA/ALT (check HIV status before starting). (4) Lamivudine – ALT/HBV DNA. (5) Telbivudine – creatine kinase (myopathy). (6) PEG-IFN-α – CBC (leukopenia/thrombocytopenia) and TSH (thyroid autoantibodies).
questions.beyond_mandell: Telbivudine CK monitoring for myopathy is drug-label/guideline based; Mandell does not specify a monitoring test for telbivudine.

cohort_answer.text: Non-serological test: Hep B DNA/viral load; ALT. Treatment: First line: tenofovir; Second line: telbivudine or lamivudine; then monitor ALT every 3-6 months following discontinuation of antivirals, if normal and no active disease, just follow up clinically. When started: If HepBeAg negative - for prevention of mother-child transmission, start in 3rd trimester (28-32wks GA) with VL >200,000 regardless of eAg/ALT, can d/c at delivery (only if reason for starting is VL>200,000 and asymptomatic) or 4 weeks post partum; if HBeAg positive, treat same as non-pregnant females. Drug/monitoring table: TDF - Cr and bone density; Entecavir - LFTs; 3TC - lactic acidosis, CBC; Telbivudine - CPK (low barrier to resistance, good for pregnancy); Interferon gamma - TSH (hypothyroid)

questions.model_answer: (1) Adefovir – nephrotoxicity; monitor serum creatinine/renal function. (2) Tenofovir DF – renal insufficiency (rising creatinine) and decreased bone mineral density; monitor renal function and bone mineral density. (3) Entecavir – generally well tolerated (headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea; can select HIV M184V); monitor HBV DNA/ALT and check HIV status before starting. (4) Lamivudine – well tolerated, main issue is resistance; monitor ALT/HBV DNA. (5) Telbivudine – myopathy; monitor creatine kinase. (6) PEG-IFN-α – flulike illness, leukopenia/thrombocytopenia, mood/depression, hair loss, thyroid autoantibodies; monitor CBC and TSH.
questions.beyond_mandell: Telbivudine CK monitoring for myopathy is drug-label based; not specified in this Mandell chapter (which notes telbivudine's issue as resistance).

cohort_answer.text: Adefovir: SE lactic acidosis/hepatic steatosis, renal exacerbation, hematuria; monitor ALT, Cr, PO4, lactate/CO2, U/A (avoid in HIV+). Tenofovir: SE osteomalacia/Fanconi syndrome; monitor electrolytes/PO4, CrCl. Entecavir: SE lactic acidosis, alopecia; monitor lactate/CO2, kidney function. Lamivudine: SE lactic acidosis/hepatic steatosis, pancreatitis, neutropenia, rhabdomyolysis; monitor ALT, AST, CO2/lactate, CBC, CK. Telbivudine: SE myalgias, steatosis, lactic acidosis; monitor CK, CO2, ALT/AST. PEG-INF: SE elevated ALP/ALT, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothyroidism; monitor CBC, TSH, LFT
